Chapter 41 - Terraform on Google Cloud and Infrastructure
Manager
Declarative provisioning, state control, plan review, managed deployments, and drift-aware operations
Learning Objectives

Explain Terraform providers, resources, data sources, modules, state, plans, and dependency graphs.

Design secure remote state, provider authentication, project boundaries, and promotion workflows.

Use Infrastructure Manager to preview and deploy Terraform blueprints through a managed Google Cloud
service.

Operate imports, drift correction, replacement risk, rollback, and controlled destruction. Why This Matters in Production
Terraform on Google Cloud and Infrastructure Manager is an operating capability, not a console feature. Production teams must define ownership, trust boundaries, failure behavior, change control, evidence, cost, and
recovery. The following sections connect the technology to those operating decisions.
41.1 Terraform Execution Model
Terraform evaluates configuration and provider schemas, reads current state, refreshes remote objects, creates
a dependency graph, and produces a plan. The plan is a proposed transition, not a guarantee: APIs can change,
quotas can be exhausted, policies can deny actions, and concurrent actors can modify resources between
planning and application. Production workflows therefore lock state, pin providers, review replacement
actions, validate policy, and re-plan immediately before an approved apply.
41.2 State, Authentication, and Trust Boundaries
State can contain resource identifiers, topology, outputs, and sensitive values. Store it in a restricted Cloud
Storage bucket with versioning, retention appropriate to recovery needs, uniform bucket-level access, and
logging.

41.3 Infrastructure Manager
Infrastructure Manager deploys Terraform configurations, called blueprints, through a managed Google Cloud
toolchain. It can preview, create, update, and delete deployments while keeping deployment records inside
Google Cloud. It reduces the need to maintain a dedicated Terraform execution platform, but teams still own
module quality, state boundaries, IAM, policy checks, change approval, secrets handling, and recovery
decisions.
41.4 Change Safety and Recovery
A safe workflow classifies plan actions into create, in-place update, replacement, and destroy. Stateful
replacements require backups, migration procedures, and explicit approval. Import is used to bring existing
resources under management; moved blocks and state moves preserve identity during refactoring. Failed
applies are investigated from both Terraform output and service audit logs. Rollback usually means applying a
known-good configuration, not reversing every API call automatically. Production Design Checklist

1. Why is a Terraform plan not a guarantee?

It is calculated from a point-in-time view; policies, quotas, provider behavior, concurrent changes, or API
conditions can differ when apply occurs.
2. Why protect state?
State is the coordination record for managed objects and can expose topology or sensitive values; corruption
or unauthorized modification can cause destructive actions.
3. When is Infrastructure Manager useful?
When an organization wants a managed Google Cloud execution and deployment record for Terraform
blueprints rather than operating its own runners and state workflow.

apply deliberately rather than editing state casually. Chapter Summary

Chapter 42 - Terraform Blueprints, Modules, and Platform
Engineering
Reusable infrastructure products, version contracts, policy guardrails, testing, and developer experience
Learning Objectives

Design modules around ownership, lifecycle, security, and blast-radius boundaries.

Publish versioned blueprints with inputs, outputs, validation, examples, and migration guidance.

Build platform products that combine infrastructure, policy, observability, documentation, and support.

Measure platform adoption, reliability, exception volume, and developer outcomes. Why This Matters in Production
Terraform Blueprints, Modules, and Platform Engineering is an operating capability, not a console feature. Production teams must define ownership, trust boundaries, failure behavior, change control, evidence, cost, and
recovery. The following sections connect the technology to those operating decisions.
42.1 Modules as Product Contracts
A module should express a stable capability such as a project factory, private service, governed bucket, GKE
workload landing zone, or observability baseline. Inputs are a public API. Defaults must be secure and
understandable; validation should reject unsafe combinations; outputs should expose only supported
integration points. Internal resource names and implementation details should remain replaceable so the
platform team can evolve the module without forcing consumers to understand every service API.
42.2 Blueprint Composition and Release Management
Blueprints compose modules into deployable environments. Pin module and provider versions, generate release
notes, use semantic versioning where it reflects compatibility, and publish upgrade paths. Breaking changes
require deprecation windows and migration testing.

notes, use semantic versioning where it reflects compatibility, and publish upgrade paths. Breaking changes
require deprecation windows and migration testing. A golden path should make the compliant route easier than
manual provisioning, while still supporting documented exception workflows for genuinely different
workloads. Production principle: Prefer controls that are versioned, testable, observable, reversible, and
explainable to the team that must operate them during an incident.
42.3 Testing and Policy Guardrails
Quality gates include formatting, static validation, unit tests for expressions, integration tests in disposable
projects, policy-as-code checks, cost estimation, security scanning, and plan review. Tests must cover failure and
deletion paths, not only successful creation. Organization Policy and IAM remain authoritative controls; module
checks give earlier feedback and more useful error messages before platform APIs reject a deployment.
42.4 Platform Operating Model
Platform engineering is a service relationship. Product teams need versioned templates, documentation,
examples, SLOs, release channels, support ownership, and a roadmap. Measure lead time to a compliant
environment, failed deployment rate, time to recover, exception volume, support demand, cost per
environment, and developer satisfaction. Remove unused variants rather than accumulating permanent
bespoke paths. Production Design Checklist

Chapter 43 - Cloud Build, Secure Source Management, and Build
Infrastructure
Hermetic builds, triggers, private pools, caching, provenance, and secure build operations
Learning Objectives

Design Cloud Build configurations, triggers, substitutions, artifacts, and build identities.

Choose hosted workers or private pools based on connectivity, isolation, performance, and compliance.

Create reproducible builds with pinned dependencies, bounded caches, and test evidence.

Operate failures, quotas, logs, artifact retention, and build-platform security. Why This Matters in Production
Cloud Build, Secure Source Management, and Build Infrastructure is an operating capability, not a console
feature. Production teams must define ownership, trust boundaries, failure behavior, change control, evidence,
cost, and recovery. The following sections connect the technology to those operating decisions.
43.1 Build Pipeline Architecture
Cloud Build executes a directed sequence of containerized build steps. A production pipeline separates source
checkout, dependency resolution, compilation, tests, security checks, packaging, publishing, and provenance. Each step receives only the files and credentials it requires. The build service account is not a general
administrator; use separate identities or impersonation for publishing and deployment. Triggers must bind
repositories, branches, tags, and pull-request events to explicit review rules.
43.2 Source, Reproducibility, and Dependency Trust
A build is reproducible when the same source, declared toolchain, dependency lock files, and parameters create
equivalent outputs. Pin builder images by digest where practical, verify checksums, restrict external package
access, and use approved mirrors.

equivalent outputs. Pin builder images by digest where practical, verify checksums, restrict external package
access, and use approved mirrors. Secure Source Manager or an approved external source platform should
enforce branch protection, review, signed commits or equivalent evidence, and least-privilege automation
access. Production principle: Prefer controls that are versioned, testable, observable, reversible, and
explainable to the team that must operate them during an incident.
43.3 Hosted Workers and Private Pools
Default workers are appropriate for many internet-connected builds. Private pools provide dedicated worker
pools, VPC connectivity, configurable machine types, and stronger network control for private dependencies or
regulated workloads. They also require capacity, quota, egress, DNS, patch, cost, and scaling decisions. Do not
create a private pool merely to hide an overprivileged build identity.
43.4 Build Performance and Operations
Caching can reduce time but can also preserve compromised or stale dependencies. Separate immutable artifact
caches from mutable workspace caches, set retention, and include cache invalidation in incident response. Use
build timeouts, concurrency limits, log routing, failure notifications, and artifact lifecycle rules. Track queue
time, build duration, test flakiness, failure reasons, and cost per successful artifact. Production Design Checklist

Choose hosted workers or private pools based on connectivity, isolation, performance, and compliance.

Chapter 44 - Cloud Deploy and Progressive Delivery
Release pipelines, targets, approvals, canary rollout, verification, rollback, and environment promotion
Learning Objectives

Model delivery pipelines, targets, releases, rollouts, approvals, and environment ownership.

Implement progressive delivery with canary phases, verification gates, and bounded blast radius.

Separate artifact creation from release authorization and environment credentials.

Design rollback, roll-forward, incident pause, and release evidence procedures. Why This Matters in Production
Cloud Deploy and Progressive Delivery is an operating capability, not a console feature. Production teams must
define ownership, trust boundaries, failure behavior, change control, evidence, cost, and recovery. The
following sections connect the technology to those operating decisions.
44.1 Release Model and Separation of Duties
Cloud Deploy manages delivery progression after an artifact has been built. A release binds a versioned delivery
configuration to immutable artifacts; rollouts move that release to targets. This separation prevents every build
from becoming a production deployment. Environment owners define target access, approvals, maintenance
windows, policy, and verification, while application teams provide release metadata and health expectations.
44.2 Progressive Delivery
Canary deployment exposes a new version to a limited share of traffic or capacity, observes it, and expands only
when evidence is acceptable. Phase percentages, bake time, metrics, logs, error budgets, and manual approvals
must reflect business risk. A 5 percent canary is not low risk when the affected users are high-value tenants or
when all background jobs use the new version.

44.3 Verification and Promotion
A release gate should combine pre-deployment validation, deployment health, functional smoke tests, security
policy, and post-deployment service indicators. Verification must query the same user-visible signals used
during incidents. Promotions across development, staging, and production should reuse the same artifact digest
while changing only approved environment configuration.
44.4 Rollback and Incident Control
Rollback is fast only when old artifacts, configuration, schemas, and infrastructure remain compatible. Database
changes need expand-contract sequencing. Operators need permission to pause, reject, retry, or roll back
without obtaining broad project administration. Every production rollout should record initiator, artifact digest,
configuration, approvals, target, timing, health verdict, and recovery action. Production Design Checklist

1. A Terraform plan shows replacement of a production database. What do you do?
Stop. Determine the immutable property and state identity, validate backup and migration, use import/moved
operations if appropriate, obtain explicit approval, and test in a representative environment.
2. How would you prevent CI credential theft?
Use Workload Identity Federation with strict issuer, audience, repository, branch, and environment
conditions; separate identities; short sessions; no static keys; and audit/alert on impersonation.
3. How do you design a useful canary?
Choose representative traffic or capacity, meaningful bake time, segmented user and business indicators,
automated stop conditions, and a tested rollback or roll-forward path.
4. What is the difference between logging and audit evidence?
Application logs explain software behavior; audit logs record control-plane and data-access actions. They
differ in source, trust, retention, access, and investigation use.
5. How do you reduce alert fatigue?
Page only on actionable service impact, use SLO burn rates, group dependent symptoms, suppress
maintenance, route diagnostics separately, and review false positives after incidents.
6. How do you respond to an exposed artifact-signing identity?
Freeze releases, revoke identity/federation, invalidate or distrust attestations, inventory affected digests and
runtimes, rebuild with a clean trust chain, and preserve evidence.
7. Why can VPC Service Controls break pipelines?
Pipelines often cross projects, identities, APIs, consoles, and external systems. Perimeter ingress, egress,
